title: Opioid Withdrawal — Inpatient Buprenorphine Induction Principles

summary: There are two genuinely different approaches to starting buprenorphine in an opioid-dependent hospitalized patient — traditional induction waits for the patient to be in withdrawal first, while low-dose/microdosing induction starts tiny doses while the patient continues their usual opioid — and knowing which conversation to have with addiction medicine matters more here than memorizing a specific dosing table, since actual protocols genuinely vary by institution.
whyThisMatters: Giving buprenorphine to a patient who still has full opioid agonist occupying their receptors can precipitate a sudden, severe withdrawal reaction — buprenorphine's partial-agonist, high-receptor-affinity properties mean it can displace a fuller agonist and drop the net effect abruptly — which is exactly why induction TIMING and STRATEGY matter clinically, and why this is genuinely a two-approach decision rather than a single fixed protocol.
clinicalTakeaway:
TRADITIONAL INDUCTION: hold the patient's usual opioid and wait until they're in mild-to-moderate withdrawal (typically assessed with COWS — see the cows calculator) before giving the first buprenorphine dose — giving it too early, while still opioid-occupied, risks precipitated withdrawal.

LOW-DOSE (MICRODOSING) INDUCTION: start with very small buprenorphine doses WHILE the patient continues their usual opioid, then gradually up-titrate buprenorphine while tapering the other opioid off.
- This approach doesn't require the patient to go through a withdrawal period first, which can improve tolerability and engagement.
- Though evidence comparing the two approaches head-to-head is still developing, and outcomes have been broadly similar between them in available comparisons.

FENTANYL: be extra cautious in a patient using fentanyl or fentanyl analogs — their high lipophilicity and tissue accumulation is a real, described cause of precipitated withdrawal even when induction timing looks textbook-correct by COWS score.

Involve addiction medicine / your consult service EARLY rather than improvising a full induction protocol from scratch — this is exactly the kind of care that benefits from a team that does it routinely and knows your institution's specific protocol.

body.text: Buprenorphine is a partial opioid agonist with very high receptor affinity — high enough that it can displace a full agonist (like methadone, heroin, or a prescription opioid) already occupying the receptor. If given while a patient still has significant full-agonist effect on board, the NET effect can drop suddenly (partial agonist effect being weaker than what was displaced), producing a sudden, severe withdrawal reaction — precipitated withdrawal. This is the central risk that shapes both induction approaches below.
Two approaches — know which conversation you're having

rows: Hold the patient's usual opioid; wait until they're in mild-to-moderate withdrawal (assessed with COWS) before giving the first buprenorphine dose

Requires the patient to tolerate a withdrawal period first, which can be genuinely uncomfortable and is a real barrier to engagement/retention — but is a well-established, widely-used approach with a long track record
Start very small buprenorphine doses WHILE the patient continues their usual opioid at its current dose, then gradually up-titrate buprenorphine while tapering the other opioid down over days

Avoids requiring an upfront withdrawal period, which can improve comfort/tolerability and engagement — but takes longer to reach a full buprenorphine dose, requires more careful staged dosing, and head-to-head outcome data versus traditional induction remains limited (recent comparisons have shown broadly similar overall outcomes with some signal toward reduced readmission with low-dose approaches)

body.text: Fentanyl and fentanyl analogs — extra caution needed

Patients using fentanyl or fentanyl analogs are a genuinely higher-risk population for precipitated withdrawal during buprenorphine induction, even when the timing looks textbook-correct by COWS score.

Fentanyl's high lipophilicity means it accumulates in tissue and can be released back into circulation over a longer, less predictable timeframe than the COWS score at any single moment might suggest.

This population:
- increasingly favors low-dose/microdosing approaches specifically to reduce this risk
- warrants a lower threshold for addiction medicine involvement, given how commonly fentanyl is now the actual opioid involved

This module deliberately doesn't provide a single fixed dosing table — actual induction protocols (specific starting doses, titration schedules, and choice between traditional and low-dose approaches) genuinely vary across institutions and are best driven by a team/service that does this routinely.

The clinical skill this module supports is:
- recognizing the opioid withdrawal presentation
- understanding why timing/approach matters
- knowing to involve addiction medicine (or your institution's equivalent consult service) early

Rather than either avoiding buprenorphine induction altogether or improvising a full protocol without that support.
